exampleAnswers.title: Determining Whether a Set of Vectors Is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product

question.text:
\[ \mathbf{v}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_2=\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{v}_3=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the vectors shown above. Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathbb{R}^3$ is defined as \[ \langle \mathbf{x},\mathbf{y} \rangle = x_1 y_1 + 2x_2 y_2 + 3x_3 y_3, \] which of the following statements are true?

  1. $\mathbf{v}_1 \perp \mathbf{v}_2$ with respect to the given inner product
  2. $\mathbf{v}_1 \perp \mathbf{v}_3$ with respect to the given inner product
  3. $S=\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
question.choice5: None of the statements is true
question.explanation:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, we have \begin{align*} \langle \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_2 \rangle &= (6)(-1) + 2(0)(1) +3 (-2)(-1) \\[5pt] &= -6 + 0 + 6 \\[5pt] &= 0, \end{align*} which means that $\mathbf{v}_1 \perp \mathbf{v}_2$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement II is false since \begin{align*} \langle \mathbf{v}_1,\mathbf{v}_3 \rangle &= (6)(1) + 2(0)(1) +3 (-2)(0) \\[5pt] &= 6 + 0 + 0 \\[5pt] &= 6 \neq 0, \end{align*} which means that $\mathbf{v}_1 \not\perp \mathbf{v}_3$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement III is false. Since $\mathbf{v}_1 \not\perp \mathbf{v}_3,$ the set $S$ is not orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

exampleAnswers.title: Determining Whether a Set of Polynomials is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product

question.text:
Consider the following set of polynomials: \[ p_1(t)=2t-4, \qquad p_2(t)=2-t, \qquad p_3(t)=1-t. \] Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathbb{R}_1[t]$ of polynomials of degree at most $1$ in the variable $t$ is defined as \[ \langle p(t),q(t) \rangle = p(1)q(1) + p(2)q(2), \] which of the following statements are true?

  1. $p_1(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  2. $p_2(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  3. $S=\{ p_1(t), p_2(t), p_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
question.choice5: None of the statements is true
question.explanation:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. Indeed, we have \begin{align*} \langle p_1(t),p_3(t) \rangle &= \langle 2t-4,1-t \rangle \\[5pt] &= (2t-4) \Big|_{1} \cdot (1-t) \Big|_1 + (2t-4) \Big|_{2} \cdot (1-t) \Big|_2 \\[5pt] &= (2(1)-4) \cdot (1-1) + (2(2)-4) \cdot (1-2) \\[5pt] &= 0, \end{align*} which means that $p_1(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement II is true. Indeed, we have \begin{align*} \langle p_2(t),p_3(t) \rangle &= \langle 2-t,1-t \rangle \\[5pt] &= (2-t) \Big|_{1} \cdot (1-t) \Big|_1 + (2-t) \Big|_{2} \cdot (1-t) \Big|_2 \\[5pt] &= (2-1) \cdot (1-1) + (2-2) \cdot (1-2) \\[5pt] &= 0, \end{align*} which means that $p_2(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement III is false. Let's check if $p_1(t) \perp p_2(t).$ Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \langle p_1(t),p_2(t) \rangle &= \langle 2t-4,2-t \rangle \\[5pt] &= (2t-4) \Big|_{1} \cdot (2-t) \Big|_1 + (2t-4) \Big|_{2} \cdot (2-t) \Big|_2 \\[5pt] &= (2(1)-4) \cdot (2-1) + (2(2)-4) \cdot (2-2) \\[5pt] &= -2 \ne 0, \end{align*} which means that $p_1(t) \not\perp p_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. So, the set $S$ is not an orthogonal set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

  1. $p_1(t) \not\perp p_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product

  3. $S=\{ p_1(t), p_2(t), p_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

  • Statement I is true.   2. $p_2(t) \perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  3. $S=\{ p_1(t), p_2(t), p_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false since \begin{align*} \langle p_1(t),p_2(t) \rangle &= \langle t-1,2t+2 \rangle \\[5pt] &= (t-1) \Big|_{-1} \cdot (2t+2) \Big|_{-1} + (t-1) \Big|_{1} \cdot (2t+2) \Big|_1 \\[5pt] &= ((-1)-1) \cdot (2(-1)+2) + (1-1) \cdot (2(1)+2) \\[5pt] &= 0, \end{align*} which means that $p_1(t) \perp p_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement III is false. Let's check if $p_1(t) \perp p_3(t).$ Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \langle p_1(t),p_3(t) \rangle &= \langle t-1,2-2t \rangle \\[5pt] &= (t-1) \Big|_{-1} \cdot (2-2t) \Big|_{-1} + (t-1) \Big|_{1} \cdot (2-2t) \Big|_1 \\[5pt] &= ((-1)-1) \cdot (2-2(-1)) + (1-1) \cdot (2-2(1)) \\[5pt] &= -8 \ne 0, \end{align*} which means that $p_1(t) \not\perp p_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product. exampleAnswers.title: Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product

question.text:
Consider the following set of functions: \[ f_1(t)=t, \qquad f_2(t)=t^2, \qquad f_3(t)= t-\dfrac{5}{12}t^3 \]

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathcal{C}[-2,2]$ of continuous functions over $[-2,2]$ is defined as \[ \langle f(t),g(t) \rangle = \int_{-2}^{2} f(t)g(t) \: \text{d}t, \] which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  2. $f_1(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  3. $S=\{ f_1(t), f_2(t), f_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
Hint: $\langle f_2,f_3 \rangle=0.$
question.choice5: None of the statements are true
question.explanation:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. We have \begin{align*} \langle f_1(t),f_2(t) \rangle &= \langle t,t^2 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \int_{-2}^{2} t\cdot t^2 \: \text{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{-2}^{2} t^3 \: \text{d}t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{t^4}{4}\Bigg|_{-2}^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2^4}{4}-\left(\dfrac{(-2)^4}{4}\right) \\[5pt] &= 0. \end{align*} This means that $f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement II is true. We have \begin{align*} \langle f_1(t),f_3(t) \rangle &= \left\langle t,t-\dfrac{5}{12}t^3 \right\rangle \\[5pt] &= \int_{-2}^{2} t\cdot \left(t-\dfrac{5}{12}t^3\right) \: \text{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_{-2}^{2} \left(t^2-\dfrac{5}{12}t^4\right) \: \text{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left(\dfrac{t^3}{3} - \dfrac{1}{12}t^5\right)\Bigg|_{-2}^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2^3}{3} - \dfrac{1}{12}2^5 - \left(\dfrac{(-2)^3}{3} - \dfrac{1}{12}(-2)^5\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{16}{3} - \dfrac{16}{3} \\[5pt] &= 0. \end{align*} This means that $f_1(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement III is true. Since $f_1(t) \perp f_2(t),$ $f_1(t) \perp f_3(t),$ and $f_2(t) \perp f_3(t),$ the set $S$ is orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

example.title: Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product

question.text:
Consider the following set of functions: \[ f_1(t)=\sin(2t), \qquad f_2(t)=\sin t, \qquad f_3(t)= \cos t \]

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathcal{C}[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ of continuous functions over $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ is defined as \[ \langle f(t),g(t) \rangle = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} f(t)g(t) \: \text{d}t, \] which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  2. $f_2(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  3. $S=\{ f_1(t), f_2(t), f_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
question.choice5: None of the statements are true
question.explanation:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false. We have \begin{align*} \langle f_1(t),f_2(t) \rangle = \langle \sin(2t),\sin t \rangle = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sin(2t)\sin t \: \text{d}t. \end{align*} We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\sin\alpha\sin\beta=\dfrac12(\cos(\alpha-\beta)-\cos(\alpha+\beta))$ as follows: \begin{align*} \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sin(2t)\, \sin t \,\textrm{d}t &= \dfrac 1 2 \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \big( \cos(2t-t) - \cos(2t+t) \big) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2 \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \big( \cos{t} + \cos(3t) \big) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\left( \sin{t} + \dfrac{1}{3}\sin(3t) \right) \Bigg|_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\left( \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \dfrac{1}{3}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \right) - \dfrac 1 2\left( \sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) + \dfrac{1}{3}\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\cdot \dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac 1 2\cdot \left(-\dfrac{4}{3}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{3} \neq 0. \end{align*} This means that $f_1(t) \not\perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement II is true. We have \begin{align*} \langle f_2(t),f_3(t) \rangle = \langle \sin t,\cos t \rangle = \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sin t\cos t \: \text{d}t. \end{align*} We can evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=\sin t,$ differentiating we have $\text{d}u=\cos t.$ Hence: \begin{align*} \int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \sin t\, \cos t \,\textrm{d}t &= \dfrac{1}{2}\sin^2 t \Bigg|_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2 \left( \sin^2\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) - \sin^2\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\left( 1 - 1 \right) \\[5pt] &= 0. \end{align*} This means that $f_2(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement III is false. Since $f_1(t) \not\perp f_2(t),$ the set $S$ is not orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

example.title: Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product

question.text:
Consider the following set of functions: \[ f_1(t)=\cos{t}, \qquad f_2(t)=\sin(2t), \qquad f_3(t)=t \]

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathcal{C}[0,\pi]$ of continuous functions over $[0,\pi]$ is defined as \[ \langle f(t),g(t) \rangle = \int_0^{\pi} f(t)g(t) \: \text{d}t, \] which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  2. $f_1(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  3. $S=\{ f_1(t), f_2(t), f_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
question.choice1: None of the statements are true
question.explanation:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false. We have \begin{align*} \langle f_1(t),f_2(t) \rangle = \langle \cos{t},\sin(2t) \rangle = \int_0^{\pi} \cos{t}\sin(2t) \: \text{d}t. \end{align*} We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\sin\alpha\cos\beta=\dfrac12(\sin(\alpha-\beta)+\sin(\alpha+\beta))$ as follows: \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\pi} \cos{t}\, \sin(2t) \,\textrm{d}t &= \dfrac 1 2 \int_{0}^{\pi} \big( \sin(2t-t) + \sin(2t+t) \big) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2 \int_{0}^{\pi} \big( \sin{t} + \sin(3t) \big) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\left( -\cos{t} - \dfrac{1}{3}\cos(3t) \right) \Bigg|_0^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\left( -\cos(\pi) - \dfrac{1}{3}\cos(3\pi) \right) - \dfrac 1 2\left( -\cos(0) - \dfrac{1}{3}\cos(0) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\cdot \dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac 1 2\cdot \left(-\dfrac{4}{3}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4}{3} \neq 0. \end{align*} This means that $f_1(t) \not\perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement II is false. We have \begin{align*} \langle f_1(t),f_3(t) \rangle = \langle \cos{t},t \rangle = \int_0^{\pi} t \cos{t} \: \text{d}t. \end{align*} Let's use integration by parts. We denote \[ \begin{array}{lcl} u = t & \Longrightarrow & u' = 1, \\ v' = \cos t & \Longrightarrow & v = \displaystyle\int v' \,\textrm{d}t = \int \cos t \,\textrm{d}t = \sin t. \end{array} \] Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain \begin{align*} \int_0^{\pi} t\cos{t} \: \text{d}t &= uv \bigg|_{0}^{\pi} - \int_{0}^{\pi} u'v \,\textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left( t \sin t \right)\bigg|_{0}^{\pi} - \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin t \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &=\left( \pi \cdot \sin (\pi) - 0 \cdot \sin(0) \right) + \cos t \bigg|_{0}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= 0 + \left( \cos (\pi) - \cos(0) \right) \\[5pt] &= -2 \neq 0. \end{align*} This means that $f_1(t) \not\perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement III is false. Since $f_1(t) \not\perp f_2(t),$ the set $S$ is not orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

example.title: Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product

question.text:
Consider the following set of functions: \[ f_1(t)=t, \qquad f_2(t)=e^{t}, \qquad f_3(t)=e^{-t} \]

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathcal{C}[-1, 1]$ of continuous functions over $[-1, 1]$ is defined as \[ \langle f(t),g(t) \rangle = \int_{-1}^{1} f(t)g(t) \: \text{d}t, \] which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f_1(t) \perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  2. $f_1(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  3. $S=\{ f_1(t), f_2(t), f_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
question.choice1: None of the statements are true
question.explanation:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is false. We have \begin{align*} \langle f_1(t),f_2(t) \rangle &= \langle t, e^{t} \rangle \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} t e^{t} \: \text{d}t \\[5pt] \end{align*} Let's use integration by parts. We denote \[ \begin{array}{lcl} u = t & \Longrightarrow & u' = 1, \\ v' = e^{t} & \Longrightarrow & v = \displaystyle\int v' \,\textrm{d}t = \int e^{t} \,\textrm{d}t = e^{t}. \end{array} \] Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain \begin{align*} \int_{-1}^{1} t e^{t} \: \text{d}t &= uv \bigg|_{-1}^{1} - \int_{-1}^{1} u'v \,\textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= te^{t} \bigg|_{-1}^{1} - \displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} e^{t} \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left(e+e^{-1}\right) - e^{t} \bigg|_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \left(e+e^{-1}\right) - \left(e - e^{-1} \right) \\[5pt] &= 2e^{-1} \neq 0. \end{align*} This means that $f_1(t) \not\perp f_2(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement II is false. We have \begin{align*} \langle f_1(t),f_3(t) \rangle &= \langle t, e^{-t} \rangle \\[5pt] &= \int_{-1}^{1} t e^{-t} \: \text{d}t \\[5pt] \end{align*} Let's use integration by parts. We denote \[ \begin{array}{lcl} u = t & \Longrightarrow & u' = 1, \\ v' = e^{-t} & \Longrightarrow & v = \displaystyle\int v' \,\textrm{d}t = \int e^{-t} \,\textrm{d}t = -e^{-t}. \end{array} \] Now, applying the integration by parts formula, we obtain \begin{align*} \int_{-1}^{1} t e^{-t} \: \text{d}t &= uv \bigg|_{-1}^{1} - \int_{-1}^{1} u'v \,\textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= -te^{-t} \bigg|_{-1}^{1} + \displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1} e^{-t} \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \left(-e^{-1}-e\right) - e^{-t} \bigg|_{-1}^{1} \\[5pt] &= \left(-e^{-1}-e\right) - \left(e^{-1} - e \right) \\[5pt] &= -2e^{-1} \neq 0. \end{align*} This means that $f_1(t) \not\perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement III is false. Since $f_1(t) \not\perp f_2(t),$ the set $S$ is not orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

example.title: Determining Whether a Set of Functions is Orthogonal With Respect to a Given Inner Product

question.text:
Consider the following set of functions: \[ f_1(t)=\cos{t}, \qquad f_2(t)=\sin^2 t, \qquad f_3(t)=1 \]

Given that the inner product in the vector space $\mathcal{C}[0,\pi]$ of continuous functions over $[0,\pi]$ is defined as \[ \langle f(t),g(t) \rangle = \int_0^{\pi} f(t)g(t) \: \text{d}t, \] which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f_1(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  2. $f_2(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product
  3. $S=\{ f_1(t), f_2(t), f_3(t) \}$ is an orthogonal set with respect to the given inner product
Hint: $\langle f_1,f_2 \rangle= 0.$
question.choice5: None of the statements are true
question.explanation:
Recall that a set of vectors in an inner product space is called orthogonal if all vectors in the set are mutually orthogonal with respect to the given inner product.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

  • Statement I is true. We have \begin{align*} \langle f_1(t),f_3(t) \rangle &= \langle \cos{t},1 \rangle \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{\pi} \cos{t} \: \text{d}t \\[5pt] &= \sin t\Bigg|_0^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \sin \pi - \sin 0 \\[5pt] &= 0. \end{align*} This means that $f_1(t) \perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement II is false. We have \begin{align*} \langle f_2(t),f_3(t) \rangle = \langle \sin^2{t},1 \rangle = \int_0^{\pi} \sin^2{t} \: \text{d}t. \end{align*} We can evaluate this integral using the identity $\sin^2\alpha=\dfrac{1-\cos(2\alpha)}{2}$ as follows: \begin{align*} \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin^2 t \,\textrm{d}t &= \dfrac 1 2 \int_{0}^{\pi} \big( 1 - \cos(2t) \big) \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2 \left[ t - \dfrac{\sin(2t)}{2}\right] \Bigg|_0^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\left[ \pi - \dfrac{\sin(2\pi)}{2} - \left(0 - \dfrac{\sin 0}{2}\right)\right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1 2\left[ \pi - 0 -(0 - 0)\right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \neq 0. \end{align*} This means that $f_2(t) \not\perp f_3(t)$ with respect to the given inner product.

  • Statement III is false. Since $f_2(t) \not\perp f_3(t),$ the set $S$ is not orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
